clue.text: Chinese dish, stupid problem

blocks.note: a dim pupil is a slow-witted one
a sum is the arithmetic problem set on a schoolroom board

explanation.surface: A Chinese dish that is causing somebody silly trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are schoolroom words — one for a slow pupil, one for the arithmetic on the board — so nothing in the wordplay sounds like food at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Chinese dish → DIM SUM: the Cantonese small plates steamed in bamboo baskets, one Chinese dish standing for the category.

clue.text: Where pet is out of favour

blocks.note: the kennel in the garden, which is where the family animal sleeps
the idiom for being in disgrace with somebody whose good opinion you have lost

explanation.surface: The spot a pet gets sent to once it has disgraced itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs as one smooth sentence and is really two senses laid end to end, the literal kennel and the idiom that grew out of it. People are sent there far more often than animals.
explanation.definitionFit: The kennel is where a pet is put, and English borrowed the picture for people: a husband in the dog house is out of favour at home.

clue.text: Rose jilted

blocks.note: got to his feet: the past tense of rise
left waiting at the restaurant by a date who never came

explanation.surface: A woman called Rose has been let down by somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter makes Rose a woman's name, and a woman is exactly who gets jilted in the picture. Read it as a verb instead and it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose → STOOD UP as the past tense of rising to your feet; jilted → STOOD UP as being left waiting by a date who never arrived.

clue.text: Walker returning stuff to woman

indicators.note: Something returning is coming back the way it went, so the letters it applies to are written from their far end.

blocks.note: to stuff a bag is to cram it, and those four letters are set down backwards
the pronoun that stands in for a woman

explanation.surface: Somebody on foot gives a woman back her belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuff' looks like the noun in the picture, the things being handed over, and is wanted as the verb for packing something tight. A marcher covers ground on foot in step with others, on a protest or in a parade.
explanation.definitionFit: Walker → MARCHER: one who marches is covering ground on foot, the walking done in step on a demonstration or a parade.

clue.text: Worries about son giving show of affection

indicators.note: About means round the outside of a thing, so one piece is wrapped round the other instead of following it.

blocks.note: he cares about it means he worries about it, and the word opens up before its last letter
s = son, the letter used on family trees

explanation.surface: A parent frets over a boy and gives him a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worries about son' is how anyone would say it, which is what hides the instruction: 'about' is the only word putting the son inside rather than after. S for son turns up constantly in genealogy.
explanation.definitionFit: show of affection → CARESS: a stroke or gentle touch given to show fondness, one of the plainest such shows there is.

clue.text: Recycle a tube to hold rope attachment

indicators.note: To hold a thing is to keep it inside you, so the words in front are keeping a run of letters inside them.

blocks.note: five letters running on unbroken from the middle of the first word across the two that follow

explanation.surface: Making an old tube do a second job holding a rope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recycle' opens the clue looking like an order to shuffle the letters and is only the place they are hiding. A cleat is the two-horned metal fitting on a boat or a pontoon that a rope is wound round and made fast to.
explanation.definitionFit: rope attachment → CLEAT: the T-shaped fitting bolted to a deck or a dock, there for a line to be hitched to.

clue.text: Fast bike referring to vehicle going uphill

indicators.note: A down entry is written from the top of the column downwards, so anything going uphill in it is read the other way, from the foot up.

blocks.note: re = regarding, the two letters at the head of a memo
the everyday road vehicle, three letters

explanation.surface: A quick bike beside a car labouring up the hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going uphill' sits naturally in a sentence about a climb and is the direction instruction. A racer is a machine built for speed — the dropped-handlebar bicycle, or the motorbike stripped for the track.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast bike → RACER: the word cyclists and motorcyclists use for a machine built to be raced rather than ridden to the shops.

clue.text: Possibly offend clients by being assertive

indicators.note: Possibly says this is one arrangement of the letters among others, so they need not be left standing as they are.

blocks.note: thirteen letters across two words, all of them reordered

explanation.surface: Standing up for yourself at work risks putting the customers' backs up.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine office worry — being assertive really does offend clients sometimes — so neither word feels like raw material. 'Possibly' carries the whole instruction while reading as ordinary hedging.
explanation.definitionFit: assertive → SELF-CONFIDENT: someone sure of their own worth speaks up for themselves, which is how assertiveness looks from outside.

clue.text: OU reacts, confused from the start

indicators.note: Somebody confused has everything jumbled in their head, and letters in that state do not keep the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: eight letters, the two capitals included, put into another order

explanation.surface: The Open University responds, and makes a muddle of it.
explanation.walkthrough: OU is the Open University, Britain's distance-learning body, so the sentence reads as a report about an institution; the two capitals are simply two more letters to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: from the start → AT SOURCE: tax taken at source is taken where the money begins, before it has gone anywhere else.

clue.text: Ancient Briton held up by longest lecture

indicators.note: What is held is kept inside, so a run of letters is sitting inside the words alongside.
Up asks for that run to be taken the other way about, from its last letter back to its first.

blocks.note: four letters spanning the gap between the two words, read backwards

explanation.surface: An ancient Briton delayed by the longest lecture of the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Held up' reads as delayed, which is what a long lecture does to everybody, and is two instructions at once. The Celts were the peoples of Britain and Ireland before the Romans landed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Briton → CELT: the Celtic peoples held Britain before the Roman conquest, so one of them is an ancient Briton.

clue.text: Get better fellows with bit of discipline

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a small piece off it, and the piece taken this way is its opening letter.

blocks.note: fellows are men, plural for plural
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Improving the men with a touch of discipline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get better' looks like it belongs with 'fellows' — recruit a better class of man — and is the definition on its own. The sense wanted is the one a patient does, not the one done to a broken chair.
explanation.definitionFit: Get better → MEND: the intransitive sense used of a patient or a broken bone, as in 'she is mending nicely'.

clue.text: Scoring feat with magician and rabbit?

blocks.note: three goals put away by one player in a single match, greeted by the commentator as the thing every striker wants
the conjuror's oldest routine, a live rabbit lifted out of an upturned topper

explanation.surface: A conjuror scoring a success with a rabbit.
explanation.walkthrough: Sport and conjuring share one phrase, and the question mark is the setter admitting the second reading is a joke rather than a definition. Football borrowed the name from cricket, where a bowler taking three wickets in three balls was bought new headgear by his club.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring feat: three goals by one player in a single game, a plain sporting definition, while the conjuring half puns on the very same words.

clue.text: Police officer in his element?

blocks.note: the old British word for a constable, shortened on the street to cop
the reddish metal sitting at number 29 in the periodic table

explanation.surface: A policeman thoroughly at home in the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In his element' is an idiom meaning happy in familiar surroundings, and the clue wants the word inside it taken literally, as a substance from the periodic table. The question mark is the only warning given.
explanation.definitionFit: Police officer → COPPER, the British word behind 'cop'; element → COPPER, the reddish metal at number 29 in the periodic table.

clue.text: Sheep returns in a boat found here?

definitions.note: The definition points at the answer instead of naming it: 'here' is the place the answer is, so it describes a location rather than offering a noun to swap in.

indicators.note: Something that returns comes back along the way it went, so those letters are set down in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a male sheep is a ram, written here from the back
the clue's own word, taken at face value
the article, one letter as it stands

explanation.surface: Sheep coming back aboard a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a' does nothing clever at all — both little words are taken at face value and tacked on behind the sheep, which is easy to miss when you are hunting for an insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A marina is the basin of pontoons and berths built for pleasure craft, so the definition names the place by the boats moored in it.

clue.text: Collier has a pound for type of water

definitions.note: The answer is the adjective that names the kind, not a noun for the liquid, which is what 'type of' licenses.

blocks.note: a collier is a coal miner
the article, taken as it stands
l = pound, the letter behind the £ sign, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A coalminer with a pound in his hand, buying a drink of water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collier' is the old British word for a coalminer, and also for the ship that carried the coal, which is the decoy. The pound is the money, abbreviated the way it was written before the sign moved to the front of the figure.
explanation.definitionFit: type of water → MINERAL: water drawn from a spring and carrying dissolved salts is mineral water, and the word says which type it is.

clue.text: Poor Mike hurried round dish

indicators.note: Something poor is in a sorry state, and letters in a sorry state are no longer standing in the order they were handed over in.
Round means encircling, so one piece is written outside the other rather than beside it.

blocks.note: hurried = ran, and the word opens up before its last letter
the four letters of the name put into another order before they go inside

explanation.surface: Poor Mike rushing about with the crockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor Mike' is the sympathetic phrase you read straight past, and the sympathy is the instruction. A ramekin is the small straight-sided china pot a soufflé or a crème brûlée is baked and brought to the table in.
explanation.definitionFit: dish → RAMEKIN: a dish in the sense of the vessel rather than the food, the single-portion pot used for baking and serving.

clue.text: Doctor in country, the last to shun issue

indicators.note: In puts one piece inside another rather than in front of it.
The last to do anything comes at the end of the queue, so what is wanted is the final letter of the word that follows.

blocks.note: the long South American country, which opens up before its last letter
dr = doctor, the title written in front of a name
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A doctor working abroad is the last person to duck the problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is nearly always the word that shuffles letters and here is simply the title, two letters of it going inside. 'Issue' is the legal word for offspring — a man dies without issue — not a matter up for discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: issue → CHILDREN: the word wills and law reports use for a person's offspring, as in 'he died without issue'.

clue.text: Boy returns the Spanish spoon

indicators.note: Returning is going back the way you came, so the piece it applies to is written from its far end.

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
'the' in Spanish is el, set down here backwards

explanation.surface: A boy hands back the Spanish spoon he borrowed.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture is a small domestic scene of something being given back, and the word for giving it back is the one turning letters round. Spanish 'the' — el, la, los, las — is worth having by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: spoon → LADLE: the deep long-handled spoon used for serving soup out of a tureen, a spoon of one particular size and shape.

clue.text: Continue moving fast at racecourse

blocks.note: to rip along a road is to move at speed
on carries the sense of keeping going, as in 'drive on'

explanation.surface: An instruction to keep up the pace once you reach the races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continue' is the little word ON, the sense it has in 'drive on', so the two halves read as one order to keep tearing along. Ripon is a small cathedral city in North Yorkshire with a flat racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: racecourse → RIPON: the North Yorkshire track known to British racegoers as the Garden Racecourse, named after the city it stands beside.

clue.text: Most important sea?

blocks.note: the chief one of several, the word put in front of the biggest road through a town
the open ocean, a noun that survives now only in poetry and old sailing talk

explanation.surface: A question about which of the seas counts for most.
explanation.walkthrough: Four letters carrying two senses, with the question mark doing the work of a join. The watery sense is old and poetic: the Spanish Main was the mainland coast of the Caribbean and then the water off it.
explanation.definitionFit: Most important → MAIN, the adjective for the chief one of several; sea → MAIN, the poets' noun for the open ocean.

clue.text: Old Scottish cauldron within

indicators.note: Within says the letters are already sitting inside the word beside it and need only lifting out.

blocks.note: four letters running on inside the word, starting after its first letter

explanation.surface: Something old and Scots lurking inside a cauldron.
explanation.walkthrough: The cauldron does double duty: it is the scenery, witches and Scotland having gone together since Macbeth, and it is the word the letters are sitting in. Auld is the Scots form of old, kept alive by Auld Lang Syne.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Scottish → AULD: the Scots spelling of old, heard every New Year in Auld Lang Syne and in 'the auld enemy'.

clue.text: Tropical bird kept area in a mess

indicators.note: Something in a mess has been left in no order at all, so the letters do not stay as they were given.

blocks.note: eight letters across two words, every one of them reordered

explanation.surface: A tropical bird has left the patch it lives on in a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kept' reads as the verb of the sentence — the bird kept its area — and is raw material instead. Parakeets are no longer only tropical: escaped flocks breed wild in London's parks.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical bird → PARAKEET: one of the small long-tailed parrots of warm countries, the definition naming the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Humble college official embracing me

indicators.note: To embrace is to take something into your arms, so one piece closes round the other.

blocks.note: the dean heads a college faculty, and the word opens up in the middle
the pronoun taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A modest college official gives me a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humble' reads as the adjective describing the official and is wanted as a verb, the thing one person does to another. A dean runs a faculty at a university or a chapter at a cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: Humble → DEMEAN: to demean someone is to lower them in other people's eyes, the transitive verb sense of humbling a person.

clue.text: Duration of swimming distance at the pool

blocks.note: how long something goes on for, measured in time
one swim from end to end, the unit swimmers count off

explanation.surface: How long it takes to swim from one end of the pool to the other.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense measures time and the other measures water, and the little word between them glues the clue into a single question. Swimmers count these; a width is the short way across.
explanation.definitionFit: Duration → LENGTH, how long something lasts in time; swimming distance at the pool → LENGTH, one end-to-end swim, the unit a session is counted in.
